title: How to Write Product Page FAQ Blocks That Rank and Cut Pre-Purchase Questions
excerpt: A product page FAQ written from real customer language does two jobs at once. Here is the workflow for building FAQ blocks that win search snippets and reduce support tickets.
body: Most product page FAQ sections are written by whoever built the page, in whatever language the brand prefers, answering the questions the brand wishes customers asked. They rank for nothing and they deflect nothing. A useful FAQ block starts from the other direction: the exact words buyers typed into a search box, a chat widget, or a review, answered in plain sentences that a search engine can lift into a result and a shopper can scan in three seconds.

Collect the source material before you write a word. Pull the last ninety days of pre-purchase support tickets and tag each one with the underlying question. Export the search queries that already land on the product page from your search console data. Read the three-star reviews, which are where specific hesitations live rather than general praise or anger. Three sources, one spreadsheet, and a count column, and the real questions rise to the top immediately.

Group the questions and pick the ones worth publishing. Questions about shipping time, sizing, materials, care, compatibility, and returns are almost always worth an answer on the page. Questions about price negotiation or custom requests usually belong in a support macro instead. Aim for four to eight questions per product, because a block longer than that stops being scanned and a block shorter than that rarely covers the hesitation that blocks the sale.

Write each answer in the first sentence and explain after it. A shopper looking for a delivery window should not have to read a paragraph of brand story to find the number, and a search engine extracting a snippet needs a declarative sentence it can lift cleanly. Keep answers between forty and sixty words, put the specific number or condition up front, and avoid repeating the question verbatim as the opening of the answer.

Use AI as a drafting layer, not as an authority. Feed the grouped questions and a handful of real customer phrasings into your writing tool and ask for draft answers constrained to the facts you supply: actual transit ranges, actual materials, actual return window. Then edit every number yourself. The failure mode of AI-assisted content is not bad prose, it is confident specifics that do not match the store, and that is what generates both refunds and distrust.

Ship the block as structured data and measure it. Mark up the questions and answers so search engines understand the pairing, then watch two numbers for a month: the impression count on queries containing who, how long, does it, and can I, and the volume of pre-purchase tickets on that product. Both should move in the right direction together, and when they do, reuse the same workflow across the catalog.
